6 guides

Plan your next release+

Releases

A release becomes easier to manage when the goal, the date and the work all fit together. Start with a plan you can actually carry out.

Choose one useful outcome

Decide what this release should help you learn or achieve. You might want to introduce a new sound, build a live set, or understand which listeners connect with a song. Write one clear outcome before you build a long task list.

Work backwards from the date

List the work still needed: recording, revisions, artwork, credits, delivery and promotion. Ask each collaborator how much time they need. Check delivery requirements with your distributor before committing to a public date, and leave room for changes.

Connect the work

Give each task an owner and a realistic deadline. Prepare your audio and artwork before delivery, then plan a small set of promotional actions around materials you already have. Review the schedule when a prerequisite moves.

Put it into practice

  • Write a release goal.
  • Confirm what is finished and what still needs work.
  • Choose a realistic date and budget.
  • Create the release in your workspace.

Keep your credits together+

Organisation

Credits are easier to organise during a project than months after it ends. Keep a clear working record of who contributed and what still needs confirming.

Record contributions early

Create a project note with each contributor’s preferred name, contact and role. Distinguish writing, performance, production, recording and mixing contributions. Ask people to confirm the details rather than filling gaps from memory.

Keep versions and decisions together

Use consistent filenames for mixes and masters. Keep delivery notes, approvals and any agreements alongside the project, with a date and version. A credits list is a record of contributions; it does not replace an agreement about ownership or payment.

Check before delivery

Compare the working record with the information your distributor or other delivery service requests. Resolve missing names and unclear roles with the people involved before submitting. Keep a copy of the final information for future reference.

Put it into practice

  • List everyone involved.
  • Ask contributors to confirm names and roles.
  • Keep approvals and agreements with the project.
  • Review the final credits before delivery.

Build a routine you can keep+

Career habits

A useful routine leaves space for the music while keeping important career work moving. Build it around the time you have, rather than an ideal week.

Start with your available hours

Look at the next week and choose a realistic amount of time for music. Separate creative sessions from administration so a short email does not take over a recording block. Leave some space for everyday commitments.

Choose a small number of priorities

Pick the actions that move your current goal forward. Break a vague task such as “promote my music” into a concrete action you can finish, such as preparing one short performance clip. Keep tasks small enough to start without a long setup.

Review without rebuilding everything

At the end of the week, record what moved forward and what got in the way. Carry unfinished work forward only if it still matters. Adjust your available hours and keep useful habits instead of adding more tasks every week.

Put it into practice

  • Protect one creative session.
  • Choose one career task you can finish.
  • Leave room for interruptions.
  • Complete your weekly check-in.

Learn from your audience+

Audience

Audience numbers become more useful when you connect them to a question. Choose a small experiment, observe the response and decide what to try next.

Choose a question and a measure

Ask something specific: do live clips encourage more profile visits, or do listeners return after a release? Choose one available measure on the platform you use. Record the platform, date and starting value so comparisons make sense.

Run one manageable experiment

Choose a format and a time period you can sustain. Use material that represents your music, and make the next action clear. Avoid changing the format, platform and message all at once if you want to understand what helped.

Turn observations into a decision

Compare the result with your starting point and note what else happened during the period. A change does not prove that one post caused it. Look for a useful pattern, then choose whether to repeat, adjust or stop the experiment.

Put it into practice

  • Write one audience question.
  • Record a starting value and date.
  • Choose an experiment within your time and budget.
  • Schedule a review.

Give every project a working budget+

Organisation

A working budget makes the trade-offs in a music project visible. It can be simple: what you can spend, what the project needs and what has already been paid.

Set your available amount

Write down an amount you can commit to the project. A budget of zero is a valid starting point. Separate confirmed resources from money you hope the project might bring in so you can make decisions from what is available.

Separate needs from options

List the work that must happen and the work that would be helpful. Ask for quotes where needed and note what each quote includes. Check the full scope before agreeing to a cost, and leave room for changes where possible.

Keep estimates and actuals distinct

Record payments and income when they happen, with a date and a short description. Compare them with your plan during a regular review. If a cost changes, decide what to adjust before adding more commitments.

Put it into practice

  • Set an available project amount.
  • List essential and optional costs.
  • Record actual spending separately.
  • Review the budget before your next commitment.

Choose your next career focus+

Career habits

You do not need to solve your whole career at once. A clear focus helps you choose the work that deserves your attention now.

Describe where you are

Take stock of the music you have made, the audience you can reach and the time you can give to your work. Be specific about what is established and what is still uncertain. Missing information is a useful starting point for learning.

Choose a goal you can act on

Select a focus that matches your stage and resources. Turn it into an action or milestone you can observe, such as finishing a set of songs or testing a repeatable audience format. Keep the intended outcome separate from actions you control.

Review when circumstances change

A goal can change as you learn. Revisit your assessment when your availability, resources or direction shifts. Keep a record of completed work and use that evidence to choose your next action.

Put it into practice

  • Complete your career assessment.
  • Choose one primary goal.
  • Identify the next practical action.
  • Set a date to review your focus.
